newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to test-fire U.S. Hawk missiles.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to test-fire U.S. Hawk missiles.

text.p: Taiwan said on Tuesday it would test-fire four U.S. Hawk missiles in the Taiwan Strait during two drills in March and April seen as bolstering the island's defences against rival China.
Taiwan also will hold an army exercise in March to prepare its troops for field operations, Defence Ministry spokesman Kung Fan-ting said on state television.
"The Fairy Arrow Operation No. 37 will be launched between March 12 and April 8 in two stages, with two Hawk missiles being test-fired during each session," Kung said.
Kung said the missile drills were annual live-fire practices with no political meaning.
He noted the army had run an announcement in newspapers, asking all vessels to stay away from the missile splash zone.
Under the plan, the army's missile command will fire into the open sea from a base at the northern town of Tanshui.
The army's field operation exercises will be staged in central Taiwan from March 22 to March 28, Kung said.
He said the missile tests and army drill were "routine practices" not affected by the February 19 death of Deng Xiaoping, paramount leader of the rival Chinese communist government in Beijing.
Analysts say Taiwan military manoeuvres are designed principally around the island's need to defend itself against its only adversary -- communist China.

Taiwan suspended its annual missile tests and other large scale drills in March 1996 in an effort to avoid exacerbating tensions with rival China. That suspension followed Chinese war games off Taiwan during the island's presidential election in March 1996.

China, which has viewed Taiwan as a rebel-held province since they split after a civil war in 1949, feared the election may be a plot by Taipei to pursue independence from the mainland rather than reunification.
Beijing has vowed to attack Taiwan if it strays from its official pro-unification policy and declares independence.

China said on Sunday it envisages spending 80.57 billion yuan ($9.7 billion) on defence in 1997, an increase of 14.7 percent over last year's budget and 12.7 percent higher than actual spending in 1996.
